blocks.content: Both ConfigMap and Secret have been mentioned as sources a container can read from, without yet showing exactly how. This topic gives the first, and by far the most common, delivery mechanism its own full, dedicated depth.
Environment Variables, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Environment Variables, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: An environment variable is a named value made available to a container's process at startup, read directly by the application code through the same standard environment variable lookup mechanism available in essentially every programming language.

In a Kubernetes Pod spec, environment variables can be set as literal, hardcoded values directly in the manifest, or sourced dynamically from a ConfigMap key or a Secret key, letting the exact same delivery mechanism serve both non sensitive and sensitive data.

This is the single most common way applications running on Kubernetes actually receive their configuration, favored for its simplicity and its universal support across virtually every application runtime and programming language in common use.

Understanding exactly how each of these three sources, literal values, ConfigMap keys, and Secret keys, is wired into a container's environment is the practical skill this topic is built to deliver in full.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731621416-915122707.png
blocks.alt: Environment variables given its own full depth

blocks.content: Three Sources for a Single Environment Variable's Value
blocks.text: Three Sources for a Single Environment Variable's Value

blocks.content: A literal value is set directly in the Pod spec using the value field, useful for configuration that is genuinely constant and does not need to vary by environment, or for values not sensitive enough to warrant a ConfigMap or Secret of their own.

A ConfigMap key is referenced using the valueFrom field with a configMapKeyRef, pulling a specific key's value from a named ConfigMap at Pod startup time, exactly the mechanism previewed in the ConfigMap topic earlier in this module.

A Secret key is referenced using the exact same valueFrom pattern, but with a secretKeyRef instead, pulling a specific key's value from a named Secret, applying identical mechanics to sensitive data as to ConfigMap data.

All three sources can be mixed freely within a single container's environment variable list, letting an application receive a combination of constants, non sensitive configuration, and sensitive credentials through one unified, consistent mechanism.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731623067-533944224.png
blocks.alt: Three sources an environment variable's value can come from

blocks.content: A Real Combined Example

Consider an application container needing three environment variables: APP_ENV set to a literal constant, LOG_LEVEL sourced from the ConfigMap covered in the first topic of this module, and DB_PASSWORD sourced from the Secret covered in the second topic.

The container's Pod spec lists all three under its env array, each with its own source, literal, configMapKeyRef, or secretKeyRef, and Kubernetes resolves all three at Pod startup time before the container's actual process begins running.

From inside the running container, the application reads APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL, and DB_PASSWORD using nothing more than ordinary environment variable access, completely unaware of which of the three distinct sources actually supplied each value.

This uniformity is genuinely valuable: application code never needs to know or care whether a given setting came from a literal, a ConfigMap, or a Secret, since Kubernetes handles that distinction entirely outside the application's own code.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1
      env:
        - name: APP_ENV
          value: "production"
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: DB_PASSWORD

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1

        - name: APP_ENV

        - name: LOG_LEVEL

            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials

blocks.content: Recap: ConfigMap and Secrets, Now Made Concrete
blocks.text: Recap: ConfigMap and Secrets, Now Made Concrete

blocks.content: The ConfigMap topic described environment variables as one of three consumption methods, without yet showing the actual manifest syntax involved. The Secrets topic made the same forward reference, describing the same mechanism applying equally to sensitive data.

This topic delivers on both of those earlier references simultaneously, since environment variable delivery works identically for both object types, differing only in which specific field, configMapKeyRef or secretKeyRef, is used to reference the source.

Seeing the actual manifest syntax now, after already understanding conceptually what ConfigMap and Secret are for, should make this topic feel like a natural, expected continuation rather than an entirely new concept introduced from scratch.
Volume Configuration, covered as the very next topic in this module, will similarly return to both ConfigMap and Secret, giving the second of the three consumption methods this same treatment.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731626886-9145819.png

blocks.content: Bulk Loading an Entire ConfigMap or Secret
blocks.text: Bulk Loading an Entire ConfigMap or Secret

blocks.content: Beyond referencing individual keys one at a time, Kubernetes also supports envFrom, which loads every key in an entire ConfigMap or Secret as environment variables in one single step, without needing to list each key individually in the Pod spec.

This bulk loading approach significantly reduces manifest verbosity for applications that read many configuration values, at the cost of slightly less explicit visibility into exactly which environment variables a given container actually receives just from reading the Pod spec alone.

A common, practical pattern combines both approaches: envFrom for bulk loading the bulk of an application's configuration, with a small number of individual env entries for values that need a different variable name than their source key, or that come from a literal.

Choosing between individual references and envFrom bulk loading is a genuine tradeoff between manifest conciseness and explicit visibility, and different teams reasonably land on different defaults based on their own priorities.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: db-credentials

code.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: db-credentials

codes.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: app-config
        - secretRef:
            name: db-credentials

blocks.content: Environment Variables Are Read Once, At Startup Only
blocks.text: Environment Variables Are Read Once, At Startup Only

blocks.content: A container's environment variables are resolved and injected exactly once, at the moment the container process starts, and they remain fixed for the entire lifetime of that specific container process, regardless of anything that happens afterward.

This means changing the underlying ConfigMap or Secret a running container's environment variable was sourced from has genuinely zero effect on that already running container. The new value only takes effect the next time the container is restarted.

This startup time only behavior is a fundamental property of how operating system processes handle environment variables generally, not a Kubernetes specific limitation, and it applies identically regardless of which of the three sources originally supplied the value.

Understanding this limitation precisely is essential for correctly reasoning about configuration changes in a running cluster, and it is the direct motivation for the alternative mechanism covered in the very next topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731628529-228466632.png
blocks.alt: An environment variable read once at container startup time only

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Expecting Live Updates
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Expecting Live Updates

blocks.content: A common mistake is editing a ConfigMap or Secret already referenced by a running Pod's environment variables and then expecting that Pod's application to pick up the new value immediately, without any restart, simply because the underlying object changed.

This does not happen. The running container's process retains whatever environment variable values it received at its own original startup time, completely unaware that the ConfigMap or Secret it was originally sourced from has since changed.

The correct way to apply an environment variable configuration change is triggering a new rollout of the Deployment, exactly the same rolling update mechanism already fully covered in the Deployments module earlier in this course, replacing every Pod with a fresh one.

Some teams automate this restart trigger using a checksum annotation on the Pod template that changes whenever the referenced ConfigMap or Secret changes, causing Kubernetes to naturally roll out new Pods as part of its ordinary reconciliation behavior.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731630095-543681109.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of expecting a changed ConfigMap to update a running container's variable

blocks.content: Optional Environment Variables and Missing Keys
blocks.text: Optional Environment Variables and Missing Keys

blocks.content: By default, referencing a ConfigMap or Secret key that does not exist causes the Pod to fail to start entirely, with a clear error indicating the missing reference, rather than silently starting with that specific environment variable simply absent.

Setting optional to true on a configMapKeyRef or secretKeyRef changes this behavior, allowing the Pod to start successfully even if the referenced key is missing, with that specific environment variable simply not being set inside the container at all.

This optional flag is genuinely useful for gradually rolling out a new configuration key across an environment, or for values that a container can reasonably handle being absent through its own internal default behavior.

Using optional carelessly, however, can mask a genuine configuration mistake that would otherwise have been caught immediately at Pod startup, so it is worth reserving for cases with a clear, deliberate reason rather than applying it defensively everywhere.

env:
  - name: FEATURE_FLAG
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: OPTIONAL_FEATURE
        optional: true

code.content:
env:
  - name: FEATURE_FLAG
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: OPTIONAL_FEATURE
        optional: true

codes.yaml:
env:
  - name: FEATURE_FLAG
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: OPTIONAL_FEATURE
        optional: true

blocks.content: The Downward API as a Fourth Source
blocks.text: The Downward API as a Fourth Source

blocks.content: Beyond literal values, ConfigMap keys, and Secret keys, Kubernetes also supports a fourth environment variable source called the Downward API, exposing information about the Pod itself, such as its name, namespace, or resource limits, as an environment variable.

This is genuinely distinct from the three sources covered earlier in this topic, since the Downward API exposes metadata about the Pod's own runtime environment rather than externally supplied application configuration from a ConfigMap or Secret.

A common use is exposing a Pod's own name or namespace to the application running inside it, useful for logging or for an application that needs to identify itself distinctly among many replicas of the same Deployment.

While the Downward API is worth knowing exists, it serves a genuinely different purpose from ConfigMap and Secret based configuration, and it is mentioned here specifically to avoid confusion when it is encountered in a real world Pod spec.

env:
  - name: POD_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.name

code.content:
env:
  - name: POD_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.name

codes.yaml:
env:
  - name: POD_NAME
    valueFrom:
      fieldRef:
        fieldPath: metadata.name

blocks.content: Environment Variable Naming Conventions

Most languages and frameworks expect environment variable names in uppercase with underscores separating words, a convention worth following consistently across an application's own environment variables regardless of what naming convention the source ConfigMap or Secret keys happen to use.

Kubernetes allows the environment variable's own name, set through the name field, to differ from the source ConfigMap or Secret key it references through configMapKeyRef or secretKeyRef, giving flexibility to maintain a consistent naming convention even when the source key names differ.

This flexibility is genuinely useful when consuming a ConfigMap or Secret whose keys were named for a different purpose or by a different team, letting the consuming application receive a cleanly, consistently named environment variable regardless of the source's own naming choices.

Establishing and documenting a consistent naming convention early in a project avoids a slow accumulation of inconsistently named environment variables across an application's growing configuration surface over time.
Environment Variables Referencing Other Variables

Kubernetes supports a limited form of variable interpolation, letting one environment variable's literal value reference another already defined environment variable within the same container using a dollar sign parenthesis syntax.

This is genuinely useful for composing a derived value from several already defined pieces, such as building a full connection string from separately defined host, port, and database name variables, without duplicating those individual values.

This interpolation is resolved by Kubernetes itself at Pod startup time, before the container's process begins, meaning the application still simply reads one final, already composed environment variable, unaware any composition happened at all.

This capability is worth knowing about but should be used sparingly, since deeply chained variable references can make a Pod spec considerably harder to read than simply defining each value independently and explicitly.

env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    value: "db.example.com"
  - name: DB_PORT
    value: "5432"
  - name: DB_URL
    value: "postgres://$(DB_HOST):$(DB_PORT)/app"

code.content:
env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    value: "db.example.com"
  - name: DB_PORT
    value: "5432"
  - name: DB_URL
    value: "postgres://$(DB_HOST):$(DB_PORT)/app"

  - name: DB_HOST
    value: "db.example.com"
  - name: DB_PORT
    value: "5432"

blocks.content: Debugging Environment Variable Issues

Running kubectl exec into a running container and then running the env command directly lists every environment variable actually present inside that container, the most direct way to confirm exactly what values were injected at startup.

Running kubectl describe pod against a Pod shows its full environment variable configuration as declared in the spec, useful for confirming the intended source, literal, ConfigMap, or Secret, before checking what the running container actually received.

A mismatch between the declared source in kubectl describe pod and the actual value seen inside the container with env is a strong signal the Pod needs to be restarted to pick up a more recent change to the underlying ConfigMap or Secret.

This two step check, describe then exec, mirrors the same layered debugging approach already established throughout the Services and Ingress modules: verify the declared intent first, then verify the actual, observed runtime behavior separately.

Best Practices for Environment Variables

Use literal values sparingly, reserved genuinely constant settings that never vary by environment, and prefer ConfigMap or Secret references for anything that could plausibly differ between development, staging, and production.

Choose between individual key references and envFrom bulk loading deliberately based on the specific application's needs, favoring explicit individual references when clarity matters most and envFrom when manifest conciseness is the higher priority.

Automate Pod restarts on ConfigMap or Secret changes using a checksum annotation or an equivalent tool, rather than relying on manual, easy to forget restarts every time a configuration value changes.

Document clearly, either in the manifest or nearby, which environment variables are genuinely required for an application to start correctly, making it easier for another engineer to understand the application's full configuration surface at a glance.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Environment variables are the most common, most universally supported way Kubernetes delivers configuration into a running container, unifying literal values, ConfigMap keys, and Secret keys under one single, consistent mechanism.

Their single most important limitation, being read once at container startup and never automatically updated afterward, is the fact most likely to cause real confusion, and understanding it precisely prevents a genuinely common class of configuration related incidents.

The next topic, Volume Configuration, covers the alternative delivery mechanism built specifically to address this exact limitation, letting mounted configuration update live in many cases without requiring a container restart at all.
Keep the startup time only behavior firmly in mind. Every configuration change delivered through environment variables requires a Pod restart to actually take effect, with no exceptions.

blocks.title: Environment Variables In Full
points: Environment variables deliver configuration into a container from three sources: literal values, ConfigMap keys, and Secret keys, all through one unified, consistent mechanism.
envFrom loads an entire ConfigMap or Secret's keys in bulk, trading explicit visibility for reduced manifest verbosity compared to individual key references.
Environment variables are resolved once at container startup and never automatically update afterward; a Pod restart is required to pick up any underlying configuration change.
kubectl describe pod and kubectl exec ... -- env together confirm both the declared source and the actual runtime value, the fastest way to diagnose a mismatch.
Volume Configuration, covered next, is the alternative delivery mechanism built specifically to address the startup time only limitation covered in this topic.
